title: Quantity of Heat
notes: Heat Q is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. For a temperature change without phase change, Q=mcΔT, where m is mass and c is specific heat capacity. A temperature difference has the same numerical size in kelvins and degrees Celsius.
Heat capacity C=Q/ΔT applies to the whole object; specific heat c=C/m is per unit mass. A 0.50 kg aluminium block with c=900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ heated by 20 K needs Q=0.50×900×20=9000 J.
During melting or boiling, temperature remains constant while latent heat changes phase: Q=mL. Melting 0.10 kg of ice at 0°C requires 0.10×334000=33400 J before the resulting water is warmed.
For an insulated calorimeter, energy conservation gives ΣQ=0: heat lost by hot parts equals heat gained by cold parts. Include the calorimeter and any phase changes when specified.
Example: 0.20 kg water heated by 15 K with c=4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ needs Q=0.20×4200×15=12600 J.

Heat that changes temperature is m c Δθ. Heat that changes state at constant temperature is m L, with no Δθ in the formula. A melting calculation often needs both: warm the ice to 0°C, melt it, then warm the water.

specificConditions: **Heat Capacity Definition:** Heat capacity $C = \Delta Q/\Delta T$ is the heat required to raise temperature by 1 K. Specific heat capacity $c = C/m$ is per unit mass (J/kg·K). Molar heat capacity $C_m = C/n$ is per mole (J/mol·K).

**Phase Change Latent Heat:** During phase change (melting, boiling), temperature is constant while heat is absorbed/released as latent heat: $Q = mL$. Latent heat of fusion $L_f$ (solid↔liquid) and vaporization $L_v$ (liquid↔gas) are material properties.

**Calorimetry Principle:** In an isolated system, heat lost by hot bodies = heat gained by cold bodies. This assumes no heat loss to surroundings and no phase changes unless accounted for. The final equilibrium temperature is found by equating $m_1 c_1 (T_f - T_1) = m_2 c_2 (T_2 - T_f)$.
